title: Mysore Builds a University and Factories

title_i18n.en: Mysore Builds a University and Factories

subtitle: How a Princely Court Became a Laboratory of Learning and Steel
figure: Krishnaraja Wodeyar IV and M. Visvesvaraya
region: Mysore, Bangalore, Bhadravathi and the Model State
moral: Prosperity grows when knowledge and industry are built together.

sources.citation: Government of Mysore, University of Mysore Act, 1916
sources.note: Founding law for the first university outside British-administered Indian provinces.

sources.citation: Karnataka Soaps and Detergents records for the Government Sandalwood Oil Factory, 1916, and Mysore Sandal Soap, 1918
sources.note: Company and state records for Mysore's sandalwood value-addition.
Visvesvaraya's public programme for industrial and educational modernisation.

panels.shot: sweeping wide shot of a palace morphing into a campus and factory skyline under a dusky sky

dialogue.text: In an India still ruled by an empire, Mysore’s king and his engineer dreamed of a state that felt like a university and worked like a factory.

panels.shot: slow push-in from high balcony onto a council chamber inside the Mysore palace

dialogue.text: By 1912, Nalvadi Krishnaraja Wodeyar IV had inherited a quiet weapon: a loyal, educated bureaucracy and a people used to reform, not revolt.

panels.shot: medium shot over Visvesvaraya’s shoulder showing reports and maps on the table

dialogue.text: Into this court came M. Visvesvaraya, engineer turned statesman, carrying notebooks from Bombay, memories of floods and famine, and a plan titled not ‘escape’ but ‘Reconstructing India’.

panels.shot: close-up on Visvesvaraya’s calm yet intense face, light from a window catching his eyes

dialogue.speaker: M. Visvesvaraya
dialogue.text: Your Highness, a modern state must think as a school, bank and workshop together.

panels.shot: wide shot of the council chamber with a few anonymous advisors faintly in the background

dialogue.text: Mysore was rich in forests, silk and sandalwood, but its people sent sons away for study, its savings flowed through British banks, and its wealth left the state as raw produce.

panels.shot: overhead shot of Mysore city showing palace, narrow streets, and an older college building

dialogue.text: Colleges stood in Mysore already, tied to Madras University and British-controlled examinations far away in the provinces.

panels.shot: interior shot of a small college classroom, students bent over papers

dialogue.text: If Mysore wanted to direct its own future, it needed not only classrooms but a university under its own law and seal.

panels.shot: medium shot inside palace library, both figures standing among shelves and rolled plans

dialogue.speaker: Krishnaraja Wodeyar IV
dialogue.text: Let us give Mysore a university by Mysore law—if we can carry the burden honestly.

panels.shot: dramatic low-angle shot of a formal durbar where the Act is being assented to

dialogue.text: In 1916, the Government of Mysore passed the University of Mysore Act, founding the first university in an Indian princely state, outside the British-administered provinces.

panels.shot: wide establishing shot of the new university buildings amid fields and trees

dialogue.text: On the hill at Mysore, lecture halls and laboratories rose; a senate of teachers and officials began framing rules for courses from Sanskrit to science.

panels.shot: medium shot inside a science laboratory, students gathered around equipment

dialogue.text: By Mysore’s own statute, examinations and degrees could now be shaped to its needs, feeding men and women into schools, offices and soon, into factories.

panels.shot: split-screen style composition: one half shows a classroom, the other a workshop floor plan on a table

dialogue.text: But knowledge without work remains paper. Visvesvaraya’s eye moved from classrooms to machines, from degrees to demand.

panels.shot: wide shot of a sandalwood forest with workers and carts

dialogue.text: For generations, Mysore’s sandalwood went out as logs. The profit travelled away with the scent.

panels.shot: interior shot of palace office, maps and charts on walls, focus on sandalwood export figures

dialogue.speaker: M. Visvesvaraya
dialogue.text: We must export less timber and more thought. Oil and soap, not only logs.

panels.shot: dramatic wide shot of the Government Sandalwood Oil Factory under construction

dialogue.text: In 1916, the Government Sandalwood Oil Factory began to take shape, distilling Mysore’s forests into carefully measured essence under state control.

panels.shot: medium interior shot of distillation hall with equipment

dialogue.text: Here, chemistry and administration met. Yields, costs and wastage were recorded line by line, turning a forest into an industry.

panels.shot: close-up of a worker pouring sandalwood oil into a labelled container

dialogue.text: Within two years, in 1918, that oil would be shaped into Mysore Sandal Soap, a state-branded value added to every drop.

panels.shot: wide shot of a small soap workshop line with moulds and drying racks

dialogue.text: The records of Karnataka Soaps later traced these beginnings: a princely state learning to move from raw material to finished good under its own name.

panels.shot: medium shot of both figures examining a bar of soap and a bottle of oil in an office

dialogue.text: These were not the works of one man alone. They rested on chemists, accountants, clerks, and a king willing to sign budgets for unseen returns.

panels.shot: wide shot of a nascent industrial town with a tall smokestack and railway siding

dialogue.text: At Bhadravathi, Mysore Iron Works turned local ore and imported know-how into steel, anchoring a new town and a new class of skilled labour.

panels.shot: interior shot of an early bank hall with counters and ledgers

dialogue.text: Finance followed industry. Institutions like the State Bank of Mysore gathered scattered savings into capital, under the state’s watchful but not suffocating hand.

panels.shot: medium shot of a polytechnic workshop classroom with young men at machines

dialogue.text: Polytechnics and technical schools supplied fitters, draughtsmen and supervisors; chambers of commerce gave merchants a common voice to meet the state’s plans with their own.

panels.shot: medium shot of both in a modest conference room with charts pinned up

dialogue.text: Visvesvaraya wrote and spoke openly of his programme. In ‘Reconstructing India’, he argued not for miracles, but for steady systems that rewarded effort and punished waste.

panels.shot: close-up of a printed page of 'Reconstructing India' with underlined lines

dialogue.text: He insisted that education, banks, factories and roads should fit together like gears, each turning the other, each accountable to public scrutiny.

panels.shot: low-angle shot of both standing on a balcony overlooking city lights at dusk

dialogue.speaker: Krishnaraja Wodeyar IV
dialogue.text: May Mysore be remembered not for her battles, but for her institutions.

panels.shot: montage-style wide shot of modern India faintly echoing earlier panels

dialogue.text: Today, when universities multiply and factories rise across India, the Mysore of 1912–1923 recalls a quieter lesson: that lasting prosperity is built not on a single hero, but on systems where knowledge and industry grow together.
